title: Taking vows as a lay person
word: Taking vows as a lay person
hookLine: what it means and how it is done, with a teacher

lines: A WEEK OF PERFECTIONS AND VOWS.
WHAT WOULD IT MEAN TO TAKE THIS ON?
cards: A Sakyan named Mahanama comes to the Buddha with a practical question. Not about rebirth or the self. Just this: what makes someone a lay follower?

Where's the line between a person who likes the teaching and a person who has stepped onto the path? It's a fair question after a week of patience, effort, meditation, wisdom, moon days and bodhisattva vows.
At some point, the listening turns into a question: what would it mean to actually take this on? Today, at the end of the week, taking vows as a lay person.

teach.b: The Buddha's answer is short. A person becomes a lay follower, an upasaka, or upasika for a woman, when they have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, the three refuges you met early on the path.
Not a robe, not a donation, not a test: a turning of the heart toward three things. Then Mahanama asks a second question: what makes a lay follower virtuous? The answer is the five precepts.

teach.h: THE FIVE PRECEPTS COME WITH IT.
teach.b: So in the text, refuge comes first, and the precepts come with it. That's still the shape of how it's done.
In Theravada lands, a person kneels before a monk, who leads them through the refuges in Pali, each said three times, and then the five precepts, one line at a time, the person repeating after him.
In Zen, a ceremony called jukai, receiving the precepts, may come after a time of study with a teacher, and the student may sew a small robe-like cloth and receive a Buddhist name.
In Tibetan Buddhism, a lama gives the refuge vow, and sometimes the bodhisattva vow too. What these three share is a teacher.
The vows are received from someone, and that someone can be asked about them afterward. And nobody has to do this to listen, sit or learn. A person can walk alongside the path for years.
Taking vows is for when the walking has turned into belonging. Which is why today's line isn't now. It's someday, maybe.

how: Lay Buddhists take the refuges and the five precepts from a monk or teacher: in Theravada by repeating them in Pali after a monk, in Zen in a jukai ceremony, in Tibetan Buddhism from a lama, sometimes with the bodhisattva vow as well.

games.q: what does “taking vows as a lay person” mean?
o: paying a temple fee to be listed as a member
going for refuge and taking the five precepts, from a teacher
joining a monastery and giving up ordinary family life

p: asks what makes a lay follower
the Zen ceremony of receiving precepts
gives the refuge vow in Tibet

s: to be a lay follower you must give a large donation
the Buddha tells Mahanama it's going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha.
in Theravada, a person repeats the refuges and precepts after a monk
in Pali, a line at a time, with the refuges said three times.
you have to take vows before you can meditate or learn
listening, sitting and learning are open to anyone; vows are for when walking turns into belonging.

games.q: you're Mahanama. you ask the Buddha what makes someone a lay follower. what does he say?
o: going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha.
games.why: refuge makes a lay follower. when Mahanama asks what makes one virtuous, the answer is the five precepts.

practice: Walk back through this week, patience, effort, meditation, wisdom, the moon days, the bodhisattva precepts, and notice which one stayed with you. Then let a question come gently: if someday I took a vow, what might it be?
The refuges, one precept, or none at all are all real answers, so don't decide; just notice where your mind keeps returning.

wordCard.voice: Taking vows as a lay person. Going for refuge and receiving the precepts, from a teacher, in front of a community: what the Buddha told Mahanama makes a lay follower. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit upasaka (upasika for a woman): a lay follower.

carryVoice: Your line: someday, maybe. There's no hurry at all on this path. And that's the week.
